server.name: youtube-transcripts-mcp
server.instructions: YouTube transcripts for AI agents. Use search_videos to find videos, get_transcript for the full transcript (text, timestamped segments or SRT) plus video metadata and available caption languages, get_video_chapters for creator chapters (or topic segments derived from the transcript), and summarize_transcript for an extractive summary with key points, keywords, per-chapter bullets and timestamped quotes. Errors carry a stable code (e.g. TRANSCRIPTS_DISABLED, NO_TRANSCRIPT_FOUND, AGE_RESTRICTED, REQUEST_BLOCKED).

tools.name: get_transcript
tools.title: Get YouTube transcript
tools.description: Fetch the transcript (captions) of a YouTube video plus metadata: title, channel, duration, views, publish date, available caption languages and whether the returned transcript is auto-generated. Formats: 'text' (plain text; with include_timestamps, ~30 s paragraphs prefixed [m:ss]), 'segments' (array of {start, duration, text}) or 'srt'. Can machine-translate captions via YouTube (translate_to).

video.description: YouTube video id (e.g. dQw4w9WgXcQ) or URL (watch?v=, youtu.be/, /shorts/, /embed/, /live/)

languages.description: Preferred caption languages in priority order, e.g. ["en", "de"]. Manual captions beat auto-generated ones. Default ["en"].

include_timestamps.description: text: prefix paragraphs with [m:ss]; segments: add a 'time' string. SRT always has timing.

translate_to.description: Optional target language code; YouTube translates the best available track.

fallback_to_any_language.description: If none of `languages` exists, return the best available track instead of failing. Default true.

max_chars.description: Truncate the transcript content to about this many characters (sets truncated=true).

tools.name: search_videos
tools.title: Search YouTube videos
tools.description: Search YouTube videos by keyword (YouTube's InnerTube search API, the same one the website uses). Returns video id, title, channel, duration, views, relative publish time, description snippet, thumbnail and badges. Optional filters: upload_date, duration (short <4 min, medium 4-20 min, long >20 min), sort_by, and features (e.g. 'subtitles' = only videos with captions).

upload_date.description: Only videos uploaded within the last hour/today/week/month/year

duration.description: short (< 4 min), medium (4-20 min) or long (> 20 min)

features.description: Feature filters, e.g. ['subtitles'] for videos with captions, ['live'], ['hd'], ['creative_commons']

hl.description: Interface language for result text. Default en.

tools.name: get_video_chapters
tools.title: Get video chapters
tools.description: Chapters of a YouTube video with start/end times and deep links. Uses the creator's chapters from the description (or YouTube's chapter markers) when present; otherwise derives topic segments from the transcript (time windows + keyword-shift detection) and titles them with their distinctive keywords and a representative sentence.

source.description: auto (default): creator chapters, else derived; description: creator chapters only; transcript: always derive

languages.description: Preferred caption languages in priority order, e.g. ["en", "de"]. Manual captions beat auto-generated ones. Default ["en"].

target_chapters.description: Derived chapters only: desired number of chapters (default scales with video length)

Let's start with sunlight itself. Light arrives in tiny packets of energy called photons, and each photon carries an amount of energy that depends on its color. Blue photons carry more energy than red photons, and infrared photons carry less still. On a clear day at noon, roughly one thousand watts of sunlight land on every square meter of ground. That number, one kilowatt per square meter, is the standard test condition every solar panel is rated against. The whole job of a solar panel is to catch as many of those photons as possible and turn their energy into moving electrons. So what happens inside a silicon solar cell? A solar cell is a thin wafer of silicon that has been doped with small amounts of other elements. The top layer is doped with phosphorus, which gives it extra electrons, and the bottom layer is doped with boron, which leaves gaps called holes. Where those two layers meet, you get a p-n junction with a built-in electric field. When a photon with enough energy hits the silicon, it knocks an electron loose and leaves a hole behind. The electric field at the junction pushes the electron one way and the hole the other way, and that separation is what creates a voltage. Connect a wire from the front contacts to the back contacts and the electrons flow through it as direct current. A single silicon cell only produces about half a volt, no matter how big it is. Photons with too little energy pass straight through, and the extra energy of blue photons is lost as heat, which is why the best commercial cells convert only about twenty two percent of sunlight into electricity. Half a volt is not very useful on its own, so cells are combined into panels. A typical residential panel has sixty or seventy two cells wired in series, which adds their voltages together to roughly thirty to forty volts. The cells are sandwiched between tempered glass on the front and a polymer backsheet, then framed in aluminum to survive decades of weather. Because the cells are in series, shading a single cell can drag down the whole string, a bit like a kink in a garden hose. That's why modern panels include bypass diodes that let current route around a shaded group of cells. Panels are then wired together into strings on the roof to reach the voltage the inverter expects. Now for the part most people skip: the inverter. Solar panels produce direct current, but your home and the electrical grid run on alternating current. The inverter converts direct current into alternating current that matches the grid's voltage and frequency exactly. Good inverters also run maximum power point tracking, constantly adjusting the electrical load so the panels operate at their most efficient voltage as clouds pass and temperature changes. There are three main options: a single string inverter, microinverters on every panel, or power optimizers paired with a central inverter. Microinverters cost more, but they handle partial shading much better because every panel is tracked on its own. When your panels produce more power than the house uses, the inverter pushes the surplus onto the grid, and with net metering your utility credits you for it. For safety, a grid-tied inverter shuts down automatically during a power outage so it can't send current into lines that utility crews are repairing. A home battery stores surplus solar energy during the day so you can use it in the evening, when demand and electricity prices are highest. With a battery and the right inverter, your system can keep the lights on during a blackout by forming its own small island grid. Batteries add significant cost, though, so whether one makes sense depends on your utility's rates and how often the power goes out. So, is solar worth it? For most homes with a sunny, unshaded roof, a solar system pays for itself in roughly six to ten years, and panels are usually warrantied for twenty five years. Panels slowly lose about half a percent of their output each year, so after twenty five years they still produce close to ninety percent of their original power. stretch and folds grab one side of the dough stretch it up and fold it over the top then rotate the bowl and repeat four times with each set of stretch and folds the dough gets smoother stronger and more elastic bulk fermentation usually takes four to six hours depending on the temperature of your kitchen warmer kitchens ferment much faster you are looking for the dough to rise about fifty percent with a domed jiggly surface and bubbles on the sides of the bowl now we shape the loaf turn the dough out onto a lightly floured counter and pre shape it into a loose round with a bench scraper let it rest for twenty minutes then do the final shaping by folding the sides into the middle and rolling it up tightly to build surface tension place the shaped loaf seam side up in a floured banneton basket rice flour works best because it does not stick cover the basket and put it in the fridge overnight for a cold proof of twelve to sixteen hours the cold proof makes the dough much easier to score and it gives the bread that deeper sour flavor next morning it's time to bake put your dutch oven in the oven and preheat everything to two hundred and fifty degrees celsius for a full hour flip the cold dough onto parchment paper and score it with a razor blade one confident slash about a centimeter deep lower it into the hot dutch oven put the lid on and bake for twenty minutes crust is deep brown finally and this is the hardest part let the bread cool on a wire rack for at least one hour before cutting it the crumb is still setting while the loaf cools so cutting it early makes the inside gummy look at that open crumb and that crackly crust that is exactly what we want if you try this recipe let me know in the comments and subscribe for more baking videos see you next
